title: Classical machine learning
summary: Concepts from ISLP (Python edition, with the exact Stanford lecture videos per section) and engineering from the scikit-learn User Guide: framing and baselines, bias–variance and regularisation, linear/logistic models, trees and boosting, unsupervised methods and anomaly detection, leakage-safe pipelines and CV, cost-based thresholds, calibration, retrieval metrics for RAG, tuning, error analysis and shipping a model safely. CS229 public lectures/notes (free; replaces the Stanford-only site) and the rest of ISLP form the Deep track. Andrew Ng's Coursera specialization is not used (free access not guaranteed; TensorFlow).

quiz.prompt: You train the same model architecture on 50 different random training subsets and observe that predictions vary wildly between them. What does this indicate?

quiz.prompt: The normal equation gives optimal weights directly. Why would you prefer gradient descent instead?
options: Gradient descent requires less memory than storing the data
Gradient descent always gives more accurate results
The normal equation does not work for linear regression
Matrix inversion in the normal equation is O(n^3) in features, which is too slow for thousands of features
quiz.explain: The normal equation requires inverting X^T * X, which is O(n^3) in the number of features. For large feature counts, gradient descent is more efficient. (Adapted from rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch Phase 02 lesson 02-linear-regression quiz.json, MIT licence.)

quiz.prompt: A random forest with 100 trees has the same test accuracy as 200 trees. Adding more trees to 500 also shows no improvement. Why?
options: After enough trees, variance reduction plateaus and adding more trees provides diminishing returns without increasing overfitting
The trees are all identical so adding more has no effect
The random forest is underfitting and needs a different algorithm
quiz.explain: Random forests do not overfit with more trees (unlike boosting). However, variance reduction plateaus once enough diverse trees have been averaged. quiz.prompt: What is the silhouette score measuring?
options: The total number of clusters found
How similar each point is to its own cluster compared to the nearest other cluster
The speed of the clustering algorithm
The percentage of outliers in the data
quiz.explain: Silhouette score = (b - a) / max(a, b), where a is mean intra-cluster distance and b is mean nearest-cluster distance. It ranges from -1 (wrong cluster) to +1 (well-clustered). quiz.prompt: A production model receives a categorical value it never saw during training ('new_category'). What should the pipeline handle?

quiz.prompt: AUC-ROC = 0.5 for a binary classifier. What does this indicate?

quiz.prompt: Why does random search often outperform grid search with the same evaluation budget?
options: Random search always finds the global optimum
Most hyperparameters have low effective dimensionality, so random search covers the important ones more densely
Grid search cannot handle continuous hyperparameters
Random search uses a better optimization algorithm
quiz.explain: Usually only 1-2 hyperparameters matter for a given problem. Grid search wastes evaluations varying unimportant ones.
